query: For rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs a strong magnetocaloric response at low applied fields while maintaining rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and mechanical stability? State one controlled intervention that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that would support it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In bulk rare‐earth‐free high-entropy alloys, a two‐stage heat treatment designed to precipitate a population of coherent nanoprecipitates with sizes below the magnetic domain wall width will narrow the distribution of local exchange interactions. This enhanced magnetic homogeneity improves the magnetocaloric refrigerant capacity at low applied fields while simultaneously preserving rapid heat exchange, low hysteresis, and robust mechanical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk NiFeCoCr‐based high-entropy alloy produced via conventional as-rolled or as-cast processing, which exhibits a broad distribution of exchange energies and heterogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a two-stage annealing process: (1) an initial moderate-temperature anneal to relieve internal stresses and promote precursor ordering, and (2) a subsequent controlled lower-temperature anneal to induce the formation of coherent nanoprecipitates with uniform size below the magnetic domain wall width.
generation.conditions: Measurements under low applied magnetic fields (≤1 T) at operating temperatures appropriate for magnetic refrigeration (approximately 100–200 K) in bulk samples.
generation.structural_mediator: A homogeneous distribution of coherent nanoprecipitates whose dimensions are sufficiently small (well below the domain wall width) to reduce local variations in exchange interactions without serving as strong pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: Tailored nanoprecipitates reduce the spread of exchange energies, promoting a more uniform magnetic phase that enhances the magnetocaloric effect by better aligning entropy changes with small field variations. Their small size minimizes domain wall pinning (thus keeping hysteresis low) while also providing mechanical strengthening via coherent interfaces that do not impede heat exchange.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a standard-annealed baseline, samples subjected to the two-stage annealing should exhibit an increased refrigerant capacity (e.g., an RC enhancement on the order of 30-40% as seen in similar systems), reduced coercivity at low fields, maintained or improved thermal conductivity (enabling rapid heat exchange), and retained or superior mechanical strength.
generation.baseline: The as-rolled or conventionally annealed NiFeCoCr-based HEA without the controlled two-stage heat treatment to tailor nanoprecipitate size and distribution.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is proposed to hold in bulk rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys based on transition metals (e.g., NiFeCoCr systems) operating under low-to-moderate applied fields (<1 T) and in the temperature range relevant for magnetic refrigeration (roughly 100–200 K). It may not directly extend to thin-film systems or alloys with fundamentally different phase behavior.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extrapolates from evidence in PMC4623812 (where Pd additions and annealing narrowed the exchange energy distribution to enhance magnetocaloric refrigerant capacity) and from findings in PMC9365696 and PMC11469235 (where nanoprecipitates below the domain wall width did not adversely affect coercivity while improving mechanical properties). The precise nanoprecipitate size distribution and the optimal annealing parameters for balancing magnetic homogeneity and mechanical stability in a bulk HEA remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk NiFeCoCr-based HEA samples. One set receives the two-stage annealing treatment designed to yield uniformly small coherent nanoprecipitates; the control set receives a standard annealing regimen. Perform magnetic characterization under low applied magnetic fields (≤1 T) at refrigeration-relevant temperatures (100–200 K) and assess thermal and mechanical properties.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) and refrigerant capacity (RC) from M(H) measurements
Heat transfer properties via thermal conductivity and heat capacity measurements
Mechanical stability through tensile or compression tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase in RC) at low fields in combination with a maintained or decreased coercivity and no degradation in heat exchange or mechanical properties compared to the control samples, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

The NiFeCoCrPdx displays a second order magnetic phase transition that is tunable from room temperature down to around 100 K as x decreases from 11.11% down to 0.00%. While the magnetic entropy change for the transition only increases slightly with Pd, the refrigerant capacity improves by nearly 40%. The latter observation is related to increasingly superlinear behavior of the field dependence of the refrigerant capacity with Pd content. This increase in field dependence may be attributed to increased magnetic homogeneity within the alloy as a result of both Pd additions and annealing, which appear to reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system. AbstractSoft magnetic materials (SMMs) serve in electrical applications and sustainable energy supply, allowing magnetic flux variation in response to changes in applied magnetic field, at low energy loss1. The electrification of transport, households and manufacturing leads to an increase in energy consumption owing to hysteresis losses2. Therefore, minimizing coercivity, which scales these losses, is crucial3. Yet meeting this target alone is not enough: SMMs in electrical engines must withstand severe mechanical loads; that is, the alloys need high strength and ductility4. This is a fundamental design challenge, as most methods that enhance strength introduce stress fields that can pin magnetic domains, thus increasing coercivity and hysteresis losses5. Here we introduce an approach to overcome this dilemma. We have designed a Fe–Co–Ni–Ta–Al multicomponent alloy (MCA) with ferromagnetic matrix and paramagnetic coherent nanoparticles (about 91 nm in size and around 55% volume fraction).
